idiom_name: scala.Option[+A] with Some/None, map/flatMap and for-comprehensions
implementation_notes: Scala ships Option[+A] in the standard library: a sealed abstract class extended by Some and None, documented as the representation of optional values, whose idiomatic use is as a collection or monad - map, flatMap, filter, foreach - with getOrElse as the defaulting exit and pattern matching as the less idiomatic alternative. A for-comprehension over Options short-circuits to None at the first empty step, and Option(x) converts a nullable Java call into None/Some once, at the boundary. The type is not enforced by the syntax, though: Any can still be null and Java interop can smuggle nulls in, so the discipline plus boundary conversion is what keeps nulls out of the core. A hand-written Maybe class is not idiomatic - the standard library type is already the classic structure - and raw null survives only at Java interop and uninitialised fields, where Option(x) converts it once.
code_sketch:
val city: Option[String] =
  for {
    order    <- maybeOrder
    customer <- order.customer
    address  <- customer.address
  } yield address.city

val label = city.getOrElse("unknown")
val ids   = maybeOrder.map(_.id).filter(_ > 0)   // combinators on the wrapper
pitfalls: Some(null) is a Some holding null while Option(null) is None - only Option(...) is safe at a Java boundary.
get throws NoSuchElementException on None; getOrElse/fold/pattern matching (or orElse for an alternative Option) are the intended exits.
A for-comprehension mixing Options with other monads needs a transformer or Either/OptionT; naive nesting of Options flattens away the distinction the caller wanted.
null still exists in Scala (Any, Java interop, uninitialised fields): the type does not ban it, so boundary conversion has to be a convention, not an assumption.
